notes.objective: Evaluate tool/agent configuration for capability bloat
notes.title: Trim tool bloat: remove, defer, or clarify
notes.gist: Every tool costs context and adds risk, so keep only tools real work needs and load the rest on demand.
points: Keep a tool only for named, real use; 'might be handy someday' is not a reason.
Least privilege: drop tools the job never needs, such as refunds for a read-only agent.
Large catalogue eating context? Defer definitions with tool search; capability stays, upfront tokens drop.
Wrong tool picked? Merge or delete overlaps and namespace them, like `asana_search` vs `jira_search`.
Tool search pays off past about ten tools; below that, plain tool calling is fine.
notes.tip: Match fix to symptom: unneeded risky tool means remove it; context cost means defer loading; wrong choice means cut overlaps. Logging, confirmations or bigger models are traps.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A[Tool config problem] --> B{Which symptom?}
  B -->|Tool never needed| C[Remove the tool]
  B -->|Too many tokens upfront| D[Defer definitions via tool search]
  B -->|Wrong tool chosen| E[Merge overlaps, sharpen descriptions]

source.title: Writing effective tools for agents — with agents

notes.objective: Analyze authentication and authorization requirements to identify security gaps
notes.title: Enforce access below the model
notes.gist: A prompt is not a lock: limit what the agent's identity and tools can reach, outside the model's control.
points: Gap: retrieval can reach all users' data and only the prompt says 'current user only'.
Check access where caller identity is known, before fetching; post-retrieval filtering is too late.
Three layers: scoped credential, minimal tool surface, human approval for writes.
MCP servers must reject tokens not issued for them; token passthrough is explicitly forbidden.
Start with minimal OAuth scopes, elevate step by step, and log every elevation.
notes.tip: Ask: if the model ignored every instruction, what could it return? Answers that rely on prompts, redacting output, or secrets inside prompts are the wrong ones.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  U[User request] --> I[Verify identity and token audience]
  I --> P{Entitled?}
  P -->|No| R[Refuse before fetching]
  P -->|Yes| F[Fetch only scoped data]
  F --> M[Model sees permitted data]
  M --> G[Human approval for writes]

notes.objective: Evaluate accuracy-latency trade-offs and justify configuration decisions
notes.title: Trade accuracy, latency and cost deliberately
notes.gist: Measure what actually drives delay or cost, then pick the lever that leaves accuracy intact where possible.
points: Streaming improves perceived speed only; total time drops with a faster model or fewer tokens.
Caching and batching cut cost without changing what the model reads; batch is 50% cheaper.
Cache reads cost 0.1x input; a 5-minute write at 1.25x pays off after one read.
Medium effort matched default accuracy at 70 to 85% of cost on knowledge work.
Reranking adds a runtime step: reranking more chunks lifts recall but adds latency and cost.
notes.tip: Watch for 'feels slow' versus 'takes too long': streaming fixes the first only. Distractors cut context or downgrade models when an accuracy commitment exists.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A[Measure dominant cost or delay] --> B{Complaint?}
  B -->|Blank screen| C[Stream the output]
  B -->|Total time| D[Faster model, fewer tokens, output cap]
  B -->|Cost, accuracy fixed| E[Cache prefix and batch]
  B -->|Cost, can test| F[Lower effort or smaller model, then eval]

source.title: Chapter 11: The Numbers Before You Build

notes.objective: Analyze observability challenges and select monitoring strategies at scale
notes.title: Observe failures that look like success
notes.gist: Most AI failures return HTTP 200, so log every session lightly, tag versions and request IDs, and watch stop reasons.
points: Wrong answers, refusals and truncation all look healthy; check `stop_reason`, not just status codes.
Log a light record for every session; keep heavy prompts and payloads selectively.
Sampling or keeping only errors loses failures that looked like successes at the time.
Every record needs a version ID and a correlation ID, or traces cannot be joined.
Streaming errors can arrive inside the event stream; SDK tracing is off until enabled.
notes.tip: Instrumentation steps are defining targets and signals; dashboards, alert thresholds and runbooks only consume data. Cost reports are lagging, not early warning signals.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Each user prompt] --> B[Root interaction span]
  B --> C[Child spans: API, tools, hooks]
  C --> D[Tag version and correlation ID]
  D --> E[Light log for every session]
  E --> F[Alert on stop reason and quality]

notes.objective: Design a RAG pipeline with appropriate chunking and indexing strategies
notes.title: Chunk for meaning, index for queries
notes.gist: Cut documents into self-contained pieces, add context to each, and index them for both keyword and meaning search.
points: Under about 200,000 tokens, roughly 500 pages, skip RAG and put it all in the prompt.
A chunk missing its definition or exception needs better boundaries, not bigger chunks or more results.
Contextual retrieval prepends 50 to 100 tokens of document context to each chunk before indexing.
Contextual embeddings plus BM25 cut failed retrievals 49%; adding reranking cut them 67%.
Stale content enters at ingestion and is blocked at retrieval filtering; rebuild cadence alone fails.
notes.tip: When retrieved text lacks the governing clause, more passages, larger chunks or overlap are traps. The fix changes what a chunk contains. Anthropic offers no embedding model.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Documents] --> B[Split into self-contained chunks]
  B --> C[Prepend chunk context]
  C --> D[(Embedding index)]
  C --> E[(BM25 index)]
  D --> F[Merge top results]
  E --> F
  F --> G[Rerank to top 20]
  G --> H[Claude answers]

source.title: Introducing Contextual Retrieval

notes.objective: Apply retrieval strategies matched to data shape and query pattern
notes.title: Match retrieval to data and query
notes.gist: Exact IDs need keyword or key lookup, fuzzy questions need semantic search, and live facts need a direct tool call.
points: IDs, part numbers, error codes: lexical match like BM25 or a keyed lookup.
Questions in users' own words: semantic search over embeddings, which bridges vocabulary gaps.
Mixed traffic: keep both strategies and route or combine them, never just one.
Fast-changing facts such as stock or balances: call the system of record, not an index.
Big table pasted into prompt: 6 of 25 right; code execution on file: 25 of 25.
notes.tip: Scenarios mixing order numbers and how-to questions test routing. Picking one strategy is the trap; for live state, rebuilding the index more often is the trap.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  Q[Incoming query] --> R{Query shape?}
  R -->|Exact ID or code| L[BM25 or key lookup]
  R -->|Concept in own words| S[Semantic embedding search]
  R -->|Live fact| T[Tool call to system of record]
  R -->|Aggregate over table| C[Code execution on file]
  L --> A[Grounded answer]
  S --> A
  T --> A
  C --> A

notes.objective: Evaluate connection protocols and select the appropriate integration mechanism (MCP, API/CLI, agent-to-agent)
notes.title: Choose MCP, API/CLI, Skill or agent-to-agent
notes.gist: Use a direct API tool for one app, MCP when many clients share a live system, Skills for know-how, agent-to-agent across organisations.
points: MCP: host creates one client per server; servers expose tools, resources and prompts over JSON-RPC.
stdio for a local server on one machine; Streamable HTTP for remote, multi-client servers.
Deciding factors: how many clients will call it, and whether state carries between calls.
Needs a live call to another system? MCP or a tool. Only know-how? A Skill.
Agent-to-agent: each side's agent alone touches its own systems; only negotiation crosses over.
notes.tip: Team skills, deadlines and preferences are distractors; they describe builders, not the integration. Many owners and consumers point to one owner-maintained MCP server everyone calls.

notes.objective: Evaluate progressive discovery vs. monolithic context strategy
notes.title: Load context just in time
notes.gist: Instead of stuffing everything into the prompt, give the agent pointers and let it load details only when needed.
points: Context rot: recall drops as tokens grow, so treat context as a finite attention budget.
Just in time: keep file paths, queries or links, then fetch with tools at run time.
Skills load in stages: about 100 tokens of metadata, under 5k instructions, files only when read.
Hybrid works well: Claude Code loads CLAUDE.md upfront, then uses glob and grep on demand.
Monolithic still fits small, stable material used every request, ideally cached as a prefix.
notes.tip: Pick progressive discovery for large or changing material and many tools; monolithic for small, always-needed context. Trap: deleting capabilities to save tokens instead of deferring them.

  B -->|Yes| D[Load instructions]

  E -->|Yes| F[Read file or run script]
  F --> G[Only output enters context]

notes.objective: Translate business problems into Claude-based AI solutions
notes.title: Turn a business ask into delegated work
notes.gist: Do not ask what Claude should do; ask who owns each piece of work and what a wrong answer costs.
points: Convert accuracy rates into error counts: 99.7% of 14,000 claims is still 41 errors a month.
Claude owns judgement over unstructured text; deterministic systems own facts, maths and lookups.
Humans own accountable decisions and exceptions, never sheer volume.
Company facts like prices or balances must be handed to the model via tools or retrieval.
Place the boundary by stakes: cost of unnoticed error, reversibility, whose name is on it.
notes.tip: Traps: improving prompts to 'guarantee' identical answers, or escalating on low confidence. Same-answer-every-time needs a deterministic component; route by stakes, not model confidence.
notes.diagram:

  B -->|Facts and maths| D[Deterministic system]
  B -->|Accountable call| E[Human]
  C --> F[Output checked by stakes]
  D --> F
  E --> F

notes.objective: Design end-to-end architectures (input → processing → output → feedback loops)
notes.title: Four stages, never drop feedback
notes.gist: Every design needs input, processing, output and a feedback loop that tells a named person when the system is wrong.
points: Input: what triggers work, its shape, and whether it arrives once or unreliably.
Processing: for every fact, is the model recalling it or being handed it?
Output: mark drafts versus decisions so nothing downstream treats a draft as authoritative.
Feedback is designed up front; it decides logging, IDs carried through, and retention.
A dashboard is not a loop. A signal must reach a named person on schedule.
notes.tip: Look for the missing fourth stage. Options calling feedback a phase-two item, or offering dashboards and logging as if someone were watching, are the usual traps.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Input: trigger and shape] --> B[Processing: owner per step]
  B --> C[Output: draft or decision]
  C --> D[Feedback: signal to named person]
  D -.->|fix and retune| B

source.title: Chapter 1: What You Are Actually Being Asked to Decide

notes.objective: Select appropriate architectural patterns (workflow, agentic, augmented LLM)
notes.title: Augmented call, workflow or agent
notes.gist: Pick the pattern by whether the path through the work is known before the request arrives, not by how complex it sounds.
points: One step needing outside facts or actions: augmented LLM with tools, retrieval, memory.
Fixed, drawable sequence: workflow such as prompt chaining, routing or parallelization.
Next step depends on the last result: agent. Costs less predictable, harder to audit.
Anthropic advice: start with the simplest solution; agents trade latency and cost for performance.
Variation you can write as a branch in advance is still a workflow.
notes.tip: Trap: choosing an agent for flexibility in a process the stem says is fixed. Step boundaries are an asset for validation, cost tracking and stopping.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A{Is the path known in advance?} -->|Single step| B[Augmented call]
  A -->|Fixed sequence| C[Workflow]
  A -->|Emerges during work| D[Agent]
  C --> E[Chaining, routing, parallel]
  D --> F[Higher cost, harder audit]

notes.objective: Design multi-agent systems and orchestration strategies
notes.title: When a second agent pays off
notes.gist: Split into multiple agents only when the work needs conflicting setups or has truly independent parallel parts; otherwise one agent is safer.
points: Valid reasons: irreconcilable specialisation or real independence. Team boundaries and org charts are not.
Splitting loses guaranteed ordering, halt-on-failure and a single audit trail.
Use orchestrator-worker: one lead owns sequencing; workers report structured results via a tool.
Anthropic research: multi-agent beat single-agent Opus 4 by 90.2%, but used about 15x chat tokens.
Verifiers should re-derive claims from source and default to refuted when unsure.
notes.tip: Wrong answers cite departments or ownership as the reason to split, or add a reviewer that approves when uncertain. Ask which guarantee each extra agent removes.

flowchart TB
  U[User query] --> L[Lead orchestrator plans]
  L --> S1[Subagent A]
  L --> S2[Subagent B]
  L --> S3[Subagent C]
  S1 --> V[Verifier: default refuted]
  S2 --> V
  S3 --> V
  V --> R[Lead synthesises answer]

notes.objective: Apply decomposition techniques for complex problem solving
notes.title: Decompose to make coverage structural
notes.gist: When output skips parts or hides where it failed, split the task into explicit steps instead of pushing the model harder.
points: Bigger model, longer prompt, lower temperature or more examples change effort, not the task.
A pass per category, such as clause type, makes a missing section visible.
Prompt chaining gives inspectable intermediate outputs; add programmatic gates between steps.
Do not split work that must carry context across steps; splitting loses it.
Same tool called over a list? Move the loop into code: programmatic tool calling.
notes.tip: Failure signature 'it missed sections' or 'we cannot see where it broke' points to restructuring. Capacity, guidance or sampling options are the distractors.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Contract review task] --> B[Pass 1: payment clauses]
  A --> C[Pass 2: liability clauses]
  A --> D[Pass 3: termination clauses]
  B --> E[Gate: check each pass]
  C --> E
  D --> E
  E --> F[Combined report]

source.title: Chapter 4: Augmented Call, Workflow, Agent

notes.objective: Align solutions to business value pillars (efficiency, transformation, productivity, cost, performance SLAs)
notes.title: Name the value pillar correctly
notes.gist: Say exactly which kind of value a solution delivers, and treat any committed SLA as a pass-fail gate before comparing options.
points: Efficiency: less time or money per unit of work. Productivity: more output per person.
Transformation: work that was impossible before now happens. Removing a role is efficiency.
Cost counts total spend, including new spend the AI system itself adds.
SLA: a number with a consequence when missed; filter out options that cannot meet it.
Hours saved with flat business output is unrealised productivity, not value delivered.
notes.tip: Check the denominator: per item is efficiency, per person is productivity. Trap: weighting a latency SLA against cost in a scorecard instead of eliminating first.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Candidate designs] --> B{Meets stated SLA?}
  B -->|No| X[Eliminated]
  B -->|Yes| C[Score on value and cost]
  C --> D{Measured per what?}
  D -->|Per item| E[Efficiency]
  D -->|Per person| F[Productivity]
  D -->|New capability| G[Transformation]

summary.tests: Whether you can split a business problem between Claude, code and people, and pick the simplest pattern that reliably works.
must_know: Claude owns judgement over unstructured text; code owns facts, maths and lookups; humans own accountable decisions.
Convert accuracy rates into error counts: 99.7% of 14,000 claims is still 41 errors a month.
Every design needs input, processing, output and a feedback loop that reaches a named person.
Known, drawable path means a workflow; use an agent only when steps depend on results.
Split into multiple agents only for conflicting setups or truly independent parallel work.
When output skips parts, decompose into explicit per-category steps with programmatic gates between them.

Choosing an agent for flexibility, or splitting agents by team or department, when the process is fixed.

notes.objective: Define evaluation metrics (accuracy, latency, cost, safety, security)
notes.title: Turn quality goals into measurable criteria
notes.gist: Before building, write success criteria with a number, a sample size and a measuring tool, across quality, speed, cost and safety.
points: Good criteria are specific, measurable, achievable and relevant, set before results exist.
Pin three things: the threshold, the sample size, and the instrument that judges.
Example safety bar: under 0.1% of 10,000 outputs flagged by the content filter.
Most apps need several dimensions at once: accuracy, latency, price, safety, privacy.
Hard-to-judge qualities stay measurable; grade them with a rubric or a model judge.
notes.tip: A bare score with no pre-agreed threshold answers nothing. Pick the option that sets a task-level standard first; distrust targets beyond frontier capability or with no instrument.

  D --> C

notes.objective: Design evaluation datasets and test frameworks using mixed methodologies
notes.title: Eval sets and the grading ladder
notes.gist: Build test sets from real traffic plus deliberate attacks, then grade with code first, a model judge next, humans last.
points: Grading ladder: code checks are fastest; model judges are flexible; humans best but slow.
Check a model judge against human labels before scaling it, and give it a rubric.
Take items from real user demand and hostile cases, never from the system's own output.
Cover rare, costly and ambiguous cases; record class proportions instead of rebalancing.
Prefer many auto-graded cases over few hand-graded ones; batch runs cost 50% less.
notes.tip: If users do things the test set never covered, close the gap before release. Confidence intervals, caveats or per-segment reporting only change how the score reads.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A[Real traffic samples] --> C[Labelled eval set]
  B[Adversarial cases] --> C
  C --> D{Can code grade it?}
  D -->|yes| E[Exact or string match]
  D -->|no| F[Model judge with rubric]
  F -.->|calibrate| G[Human labels on a sample]

notes.objective: Conduct A/B testing and iterative improvements
notes.title: Run clean A/B tests, then roll out
notes.gist: Change one thing per arm, fix the question and sample size up front, prove it offline, then expose a small slice.
points: Lock two things before running: the exact question and the sample size.
One change per arm; a bundled arm's win cannot be attributed to anything.
Stopping when the line looks good is the 50-session winner anti-pattern.
Validate offline first, then cap and monitor live exposure to a small slice.
Keep random assignment and track cost too; a variant may win by spending more.
notes.tip: When a new prompt and a model upgrade ship in one arm, the right answer isolates one change. Also reject winners declared on small samples or after peeking.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Fix question and sample size] --> B[Offline eval on task set]
  B --> C{Beats baseline?}
  C -->|no| D[Iterate one change]
  D --> B
  C -->|yes| E[Capped live exposure]
  E --> F[Monitor quality and cost]
  F --> G[Full rollout]

notes.objective: Diagnose system issues (prompt failure, hallucinations, model mismatch)
notes.title: Find the broken layer before fixing
notes.gist: Match the symptom to the layer: retrieval, prompt, model choice or serving infrastructure, using the content of failing requests, not counters.
points: Confident wrong answers after a data refresh point to retrieval returning stale chunks.
Diagnose quality with prompts, retrieved chunks, responses and tool results; latency and error rates look unchanged.
Hallucination fixes: allow 'I don't know', quote sources first, cite and verify claims.
Behaviour shift on a pinned model ID usually means infrastructure changed, not the weights.
One bad report: sample recent output to get a rate before reacting.
notes.tip: Pick the cause the scenario's trigger explains. A document refresh points to retrieval; changed behaviour on a stable model ID points to infrastructure, not silent weight swaps.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A[Symptom in production] --> B{What changed?}
  B -->|data refresh| C[Check retrieval and index]
  B -->|prompt edit| D[Run regression evals]
  B -->|nothing, same model ID| E[Infra update: router, classifiers]
  B -->|new kind of request| F[Check model fit and coverage]

notes.objective: Optimize token usage, latency, and cost-performance trade-offs
notes.title: Cut cost and latency without losing quality
notes.gist: Measure where tokens and time go, then use levers that leave the model's input unchanged before trimming context or downsizing.
points: Caching and batching cut cost without changing what the model reads.
Cache read costs 0.1x input; 5-minute write 1.25x; 1-hour write 2x.
Batch API: 50% off, most batches finish within an hour, 24-hour expiry.
Real latency cuts: a faster model like Haiku, fewer tokens in and out, a `max_tokens` cap.
Streaming only improves perceived speed; total completion time stays the same.
notes.tip: When an accuracy commitment exists, prefer caching or batching over trimming context or a smaller model. Streaming fixes a blank screen, not end-to-end time.

flowchart LR

  B -->|yes| C[Prompt caching]
  B -->|no| D{Needs a real-time answer?}
  D -->|no| E[Batch API, 50% off]
  D -->|yes| F[Faster model, fewer tokens]
  F --> G[Stream for perceived speed]

notes.objective: Monitor system performance using logging and observability tools
notes.title: Monitor failures that look like success
notes.gist: Most LLM failures return a normal 200, so log every request lightly, keep join keys, and watch content-level signals.
points: Wrong answers, refusals, truncation and stale retrieval all look healthy to standard monitoring.
Keep a light record for every session and full payloads selectively; never sample sessions away.
Always emit version and correlation IDs, or incidents cannot be traced or joined.
Read `stop_reason`: refusal, `max_tokens` and `tool_use` are not HTTP errors.
Usage reports group by model, workspace and key; 1-minute buckets suit real-time monitoring.
notes.tip: Instrumentation starts with reliability targets and signal definitions. Dashboards, alert thresholds and runbooks consume data, so they are the trap when asked what to set up first.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Request] --> B[Light log every session]
  B -.-> G[Full payloads kept selectively]
  B --> C[Version and correlation IDs]

summary.tests: Whether you can define measurable success, build and grade eval sets, run clean experiments, find the failing layer and cut cost safely.
must_know: Success criteria pin a threshold, a sample size and the judging instrument, set before results exist.
Grading ladder: code checks first, a rubric model judge validated against humans next, humans last.
Build eval sets from real traffic and hostile cases, never from the system's own output.
A/B tests: one change per arm, question and sample size locked up front, offline before live.
Match symptom to layer: confident wrong answers after a data refresh point to retrieval.
Caching and batching cut cost without changing the model's input; the Batch API is 50% off.
Streaming only improves perceived speed; real latency cuts are a faster model, fewer tokens, `max_tokens`.
traps: Declaring a winner after peeking or on a small sample, or bundling prompt and model changes together.
Trimming context or downsizing the model despite an accuracy commitment, when caching or batching would do.
Setting up dashboards or alert thresholds first, before defining reliability targets and signals.

notes.objective: Identify risks, limitations, and failure modes of LLM systems
notes.title: Failure modes intrinsic to LLMs
notes.gist: An LLM-specific risk is one that disappears if you remove the model: fluent wrong answers, inconsistency, refusals, injection and leaks.
points: Test: strip the model out; if the failure remains, it is an ordinary bug.
Intrinsic: confident hallucination, two runs answering differently, refusing legitimate work.
Exfiltration needs both attacker text in the instruction channel and an outbound path.
Prompt leaks: keep secrets out of prompts, filter outputs; over-hardening can hurt quality.
Refusals return HTTP 200; cyber and bio classifiers can trigger on benign work.
notes.tip: Asked for inherent LLM risks, pick fluent wrong output and inconsistent answers. Timeouts, budget growth, credential needs and misconfigurations are ordinary engineering risks, the usual distractors.

Transaction size and promised savings are not routing axes.
Write triggers before cases arrive; clock windows and every-Nth sampling fail consistency.
Give reviewers citations and structured outputs so they verify against sources fast.

notes.title: GDPR, HIPAA, FedRAMP: matching Claude controls
notes.gist: Each regime asks something different: GDPR lawful purpose and minimisation, HIPAA a BAA for PHI, FedRAMP an authorised government cloud.
points: GDPR: settle lawful basis, purpose and data-subject rights first; minimise personal data sent.
Residency: `inference_geo` is `us` or `global`; US-only costs 1.1x; workspace geo is permanent.
HIPAA: sign the BAA and enable HIPAA readiness; the API returns 400 on ineligible features.
ZDR: nothing stored after the response, but ineligible features like Batch are not blocked.
FedRAMP High and DoD IL4/5: Claude via Amazon Bedrock GovCloud; Vertex AI for FedRAMP High.
notes.tip: PHI in scope means HIPAA readiness, not ZDR; a region setting alone never makes processing lawful. Never put PHI in JSON schemas; HIPAA enablement is permanent.

notes.title: Bias, fairness and transparency in practice
notes.gist: Measure fairness on outcomes per group, tell users mid-conversation they face an AI with a route to a human, and assign accountability.
points: Fairness is measured on group slices of outcomes, not argued from removed inputs.
Proxies leak protected attributes; test matched profiles across groups on a schedule.
Check error-rate parity, not just approval-rate parity; wrongful refusals are the injury.
Matching past human decisions measures fidelity, and can copy their bias accurately.

notes.tip: A model card or terms page is not user transparency. Compliant and fast can still fail ethics; pick answers about skewed outputs and accountability.

notes.objective: Conduct structured discovery and requirement gathering
notes.title: Discovery is elicitation, not conversation
notes.gist: Separate the solution someone asked for from the real problem, and dig out constraints people never think to mention.
points: Done only when agreed in writing: measured baseline, dated target, binding constraints, named owner.
Ask about exceptions and workarounds, not just the happy path, to find embarrassing constraints.
Invite owners of each constraint category: legal, security, operations, finance, frontline staff.
Probe words like just, only, simply, basically: ask what happens when they fail.
Non-functional test: if it still makes sense on another system, like latency or residency.
notes.tip: Prototypes, prompt drafts, model picks and screen designs are build work, not discovery. A late constraint is an elicitation defect, not a difficult client.

notes.objective: Communicate architectural decisions and trade-offs
notes.title: Brief top-down, record the rejected options
notes.gist: Lead with the decision and its business impact, then the technical reasoning, so sponsors can approve and engineers can build.
points: Omitting the rationale turns a decision into a directive nobody can defend or adapt.
Decision record substance: rationale with criteria, plus the rejected alternatives. Templates are packaging.
Justify with lasting properties: freshness, traceability, lag. Price-only arguments expire.
Evidence contradicts the sponsor? Show it to the decision owner and let them decide.
Avoid uninformed approval: a yes from someone given nothing that could prompt a no.
notes.tip: Wrong answers pick one audience, cut rejected options for brevity, or quietly proceed or override the sponsor. You owe the owner information, not agreement.

notes.objective: Manage stakeholder feedback loops and expectation alignment (including SLAs)
notes.title: Measurable SLAs and loops that reach people
notes.gist: Turn impossible demands into measured, agreed targets with remedies, and make sure failure signals actually reach a named person.
points: Offer a bounded choice with the trade-off visible; never accept or drop targets for them.
Rewrite 'zero errors' as eval-set criteria plus handling sized to each mistake's cost.
Good SLA: quality number on an agreed eval set, plus what is owed if missed.
Bad SLA clauses: absolute correctness, which model is used, how autonomous it runs.
Scope change: show cost when requested, reset the plan when accepted.
notes.tip: Trap: tuning temperature or model tier to answer an expectation problem, or sending reports more often. Fix what the report measures and what the stakeholder expects.

notes.gist: Choose the cheapest, fastest Claude model that clears a measured quality bar, matching capability to how hard the task really is.

notes.objective: Design system prompts, templates, and guardrails
notes.title: System prompts as durable components
notes.gist: A system prompt sets Claude's role and rules; write it clearly, structure it with tags, and keep variable inputs in separate slots.
points: Golden rule: if a colleague with little context would be confused, Claude will be too.
Explain why a rule matters; Claude generalises from the reason, not just the rule.
Templates: fixed instructions plus tagged slots like `context` and `input`; keep the static part byte-stable.
Delete contradictory instructions; precedence notes, bold text or lower temperature leave both rules live.
Guardrails: untrusted content only in tool results, declared untrusted; last-turn prefill returns 400 on 4.6+.
notes.tip: When a rule is ignored, fix its placement and separation or delete the conflicting rule. Repeating it, CAPS emphasis or tweaking temperature is the usual distractor.

notes.objective: Apply prompt engineering techniques (zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought)
notes.title: Zero-shot, few-shot and chain-of-thought
notes.gist: Start zero-shot, add a few varied examples to lock format, and use thinking for multi-step reasoning.
points: Zero-shot: clear, specific instructions only; test this first with the best model.
Few-shot: a few relevant, diverse examples in `example` tags steer format, tone and structure.
Prefer a small set of canonical examples over a long laundry list of edge-case rules.
Chain-of-thought: on Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Fable 5.1, rely on built-in thinking and `effort`.
Manual CoT in tags is a fallback when thinking is off; those models may decline it.
notes.tip: Questions pair a symptom with a technique: inconsistent format needs examples, weak multi-step reasoning needs thinking or higher effort. Trap: forcing written reasoning on always-thinking models.

notes.objective: Optimize context windows and manage token usage
notes.title: Treat context as a finite budget
notes.gist: Everything you send uses the window and accuracy drops as it fills, so send the smallest set of high-signal tokens.
points: Counts toward window: system prompt, messages, tool results, tool definitions, output and thinking.
Cached prefixes still occupy the window; caching changes the price, not the size.
Context rot: recall degrades as tokens grow, so cut volume rather than reorder it.
Long runs: compaction summarises, context editing clears old tool results, subagents return short summaries.
Count with the free `count_tokens` API; recount for Claude 4.7+, whose tokenizer yields about 30% more.
notes.tip: If cost and mid-document recall both degrade, the cause is volume: retrieve or trim per request. Reordering, emphasis or a bigger window are the trap answers.

notes.objective: Implement prompt reuse strategies (caching, modular prompts, Skills)
notes.title: Reuse prompts: caching, modules, Skills
notes.gist: Put stable content first and cache it, build prompts from shared versioned pieces, and package procedures as Skills that load on demand.
points: Cache order is tools, system, messages; a change invalidates that level and everything after.
Prices: 5-min write 1.25x, 1-hour write 2x, read 0.1x base input, 0.05x on Opus/Sonnet 5.5.
Breakpoint goes on the last identical block; a timestamp or ID before it kills every hit.
Minimum cacheable prefix: 512 tokens on the current lineup; up to 4 free breakpoints.
Skills: about 100 tokens of metadata always loaded, body when triggered; pin versions in production.
notes.tip: Classic item: a large repeated prefix plus a short varying message means static content first, then caching. Traps: truncating, moving it to few-shot, or caching output-heavy workloads.

notes.gist: Before touching config, check what actually loaded and gather evidence that separates the likely causes, keeping the broken state intact.
points: `/status` names active settings sources; `/hooks` lists hooks by event; `Ctrl+O` shows hook outcomes.
Hook never fires? Matchers are case-sensitive; a misspelled tool name silently matches nothing.
Hook JSON ignored? Shell profile output before the JSON, or fields outside `hookSpecificOutput`.
Access denied: tell a policy block from a misconfigured rule before widening any permission.
Truncated answer with no HTTP error: check `stop_reason`, such as `model_context_window_exceeded`.
notes.tip: Pick the cheapest observation that tells hypotheses apart. Wrong answers change settings, widen access, restart or escalate first, destroying the evidence you needed.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  S([Symptom]) --> O[Check what loaded: /status, /hooks]
  O --> H[List hypotheses by layer]
  H --> T[Cheapest test that separates them]
  T --> F{Faulty layer found?}
  F -->|no| T
  F -->|yes| C[Change one thing]
  C --> V([Verify and record the fix])

source.title: Chapter 21: Team Enablement and the Debugging Loop

summary.tests: Whether you can roll Claude Code out to a team with the right settings layers, CI automation and an evidence-first debugging habit.
must_know: Precedence high to low: managed, `--settings`, `settings.local.json`, project `settings.json`, user settings.
Commit `.claude/settings.json` and CLAUDE.md so every clone shares permissions, hooks and project context.
Only managed settings stop people turning a rule off; list keys like `permissions.allow` merge.
CLAUDE.md is context, not enforcement; a `PreToolUse` hook blocks actions, even in bypass mode.
Automate PR review and triage in CI as line comments; branch protection and human approval stay.
Observe first: `/status` shows settings sources, `/hooks` lists hooks, `Ctrl+O` shows hook outcomes.
Hook matchers are case-sensitive; for a truncated answer check `stop_reason`, not HTTP status.
traps: Relying on a CLAUDE.md rule as a guarantee, or assuming a committed file cannot be overridden.
Changing settings, widening access or restarting before observing, destroying the evidence you needed.
Granting the review bot merge rights, or counting sessions and accepted lines as productivity.
